label: Health informatics and clinical IT
description: The clinical IT desk of a hospital or health system: CIO, CMIO, CNIO, EHR and interface analysts, health information management and clinical engineering, and the informatics programs that train them. It is the same organization as the healthcare profile seen from the systems side: the exercise stays inside the hospital incident command, the failure is a clinical system, and the decisions are about downtime procedures, restore order, data integrity and reconciliation. Plans: the CMS emergency preparedness exercises (42 CFR 482.15(d)), Joint Commission EM.16.01.01 and the HIPAA Security Rule contingency plan (45 CFR 164.308(a)(7)). Use together with healthcare for a full hospital exercise. All patients, people and organizations in exercises are fictional.

vocabulary.facility: the hospital campus and its clinical systems
vocabulary.frontline: unit clerks, charge nurses, registration staff, laboratory and pharmacy technologists, EHR analysts, interface analysts, biomedical technicians
vocabulary.operationsCenter: the downtime command post and the Hospital Command Center (HCC)

it: electronic health record (EHR) and read-only business continuity viewer
registration, ADT and master patient index
computerized order entry (CPOE) and results review
electronic medication administration record (eMAR) with barcode scanning
bed management and patient flow board
ot: networked infusion pumps and drug libraries

roles.name: Chief Information Officer
roles.team: Team A: Command and IT leadership
roles.description: Declares downtime, sets the restore sequence, escalates to vendors and owns spending authority.

roles.name: Chief Medical Information Officer
roles.description: Decides which clinical workflows are unsafe on paper, signs off order-set and alert changes and approves return to normal.

roles.name: Chief Nursing Information Officer
roles.description: Owns nursing downtime workflows, medication administration safeguards and unit readiness for paper and recovery.

roles.name: Downtime Coordinator (EHR Command Lead)
roles.description: Runs the downtime command post: prints and distributes forms, tracks unit status and schedules back-entry.

roles.name: Clinical Informaticist / EHR Analyst
roles.description: Produces report-based downtime data, fixes build issues and validates systems after recovery.

roles.name: Interface / Integration Analyst
roles.description: Handles queues, replays or discards messages and sets the interface restart order.

roles.name: Chief Information Security Officer
roles.description: Owns containment, isolation, forensics and which systems may reconnect.

roles.name: Health Information Management Director
roles.description: Owns the legal record: paper scanning and indexing, release of information and record integrity.

roles.name: Director of Clinical Engineering
roles.description: Owns device isolation, manual alternatives and vendor patch windows.

roles.name: Laboratory, Radiology and Pharmacy IT Liaison
roles.description: Runs manual result reporting, critical result call-backs and dispensing cabinet override.

roles.name: Patient Access / Registration Manager
roles.description: Runs downtime registration, allocates record numbers and prevents duplicates.

roles.name: Chief Privacy Officer
roles.description: Runs the breach risk assessment and the notification clocks.

roles.name: Administrator on Call (House Supervisor)
roles.team: Team A: Command and IT leadership
roles.description: Makes operational decisions at night: diversion, resource moves and escalation to the command center.

roles.name: Patient Safety Officer
roles.description: Collects event reports during downtime, captures near misses and leads the post-recovery safety review.

roles.name: Public Information Officer
roles.description: Owns patient and family messaging about the outage, the patient-portal banner and the press.

roles.name: Faculty Facilitator (Informatics Program Lab)
roles.description: Facilitates the lab exercise, plays the vendor and the SimCell and runs the debrief.

roles.name: Student Analyst (Informatics Program Lab)
roles.description: Plays an EHR or interface analyst on a synthetic hospital with no access to real systems.

outsideParties: the EHR vendor and cloud host
the managed security provider and incident response firm
the cyber insurer and breach counsel
the healthcare coalition and neighboring hospitals

addedThreatFamilies.label: EHR downtime (planned or unplanned)
addedThreatFamilies.description: The electronic health record is unavailable or read-only for hours or days. The question is not only how to restore it but how to keep care safe on paper, in what order to bring systems back, and how to reconcile what was written on paper.

phaseArc.title: Detect and declare
phaseArc.goal: Ambiguity: slow screens and failed logins become a decision to declare downtime, and someone must say which systems and for how long.
beats: A unit clerk reports that the patient list will not load
A helpdesk spike with a mix of real and unrelated tickets
The vendor status page is green while the hospital sees errors
The downtime coordinator asks for a formal declaration

phaseArc.title: Paper workflows
phaseArc.goal: Units switch to downtime procedures; the first hour shows which forms, reports and labels are missing or stale.
beats: Printed downtime reports are hours old (the as-of time matters)
A unit cannot find its order sheets or patient labels
A critical result is phoned, not mailed, and the call-back is missed
Registration allocates record numbers by hand

phaseArc.title: Sustain and decide
phaseArc.goal: Shifts two and three: paper backlog grows, workarounds drift, and leaders must choose the restore order.
beats: Laboratory and pharmacy manual workarounds diverge
The restore sequence is argued: EHR first, or interfaces first
A clinical leader asks which results can be trusted
Staffing for back-entry competes with patient care

phaseArc.title: Restore and reconcile
phaseArc.goal: Systems return in stages; results and orders queue; paper is back-entered and discrepancies surface.
beats: The interface queue replays and a result lands on the wrong patient
Two units disagree on what was already given
A duplicate record is created during back-entry
The facilitator closes reconciliation and the return to normal is declared

decisionPointExamples: declare downtime now with partial information, or wait for the vendor estimate
bring the EHR up read-only now, or hold until interfaces are verified
release queued results immediately, or hold them until validated
extend paper procedures another shift, or restore with known gaps
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a vendor status note, an error-rate graph, a helpdesk ticket cluster, a failed interface heartbeat, a login error text
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a downtime report that is hours old, a printer out of label stock, a read-only viewer that lags the live system, an interface queue that replays duplicates, a backlog of paper to back-enter
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the EHR vendor and the hospital command center (HICS)
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Keep clinical content plausible and marked as exercise content. Every downtime report carries its as-of time and the printing system; read-only viewers show their data age; critical results are phoned.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Interface failure or message loss
addedThreatFamilies.description: An interface engine or a feed stops, delays, duplicates or corrupts messages between the EHR and the lab, pharmacy, radiology, devices or outside parties. Orders and results may be missing without anyone noticing.

phaseArc.title: A quiet gap
phaseArc.goal: Ambiguity: results that should have arrived have not, and each department sees only its own symptom.
beats: A physician asks why morning labs are not back
The lab says it sent them; the EHR shows nothing
A queue depth number is climbing on an interface dashboard
An analyst sees a connection reset in the engine log

phaseArc.title: Size the loss
phaseArc.goal: The team finds which feeds and message classes are affected and how many orders and results are at risk.
beats: The error queue holds mixed message types
A pharmacy order was received twice
A radiology report is stuck behind a malformed message
A decision: hold, replay or discard a message class

phaseArc.title: Safe workaround
phaseArc.goal: Manual result reporting starts while the interface is repaired, and each repair choice trades speed for safety.
beats: Critical results are phoned from the lab
A vendor patch is offered with a restart window
Replaying the queue would reorder results
A nurse questions a result with a time stamp from yesterday

phaseArc.title: Replay and verify
phaseArc.goal: The queue drains; the team checks that nothing was lost, duplicated or attached to the wrong patient.
beats: A count of sent versus received does not match
A duplicate order surfaces after replay
The team signs off per feed
A safety event report is filed

decisionPointExamples: replay the full error queue now and risk duplicates and reordering, or triage by message class and delay results
discard a corrupted message class and record the orders at risk, or hold it for the vendor
restart the engine in business hours, or wait for the overnight window
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: an engine log line, a queue depth trend, a message control id gap, a heartbeat that stopped, a counts-do-not-match report
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a malformed message that blocks the queue, a vendor that needs a ticket and a signed request, a replay that reorders results, a restart that drops in-flight messages
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the interface engine vendor and the laboratory, pharmacy and radiology leads
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Raw HL7 v2 and FHIR content must be syntactically valid and match its decoded view. Use synthetic patients only.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Patient identity overlay or duplicate
addedThreatFamilies.description: Two patients share a record, or one patient has two, after a merge, a registration error or a downtime allocation. Results, allergies and medications may sit in the wrong chart.

phaseArc.title: A mismatch
phaseArc.goal: Ambiguity: a clinician notices a result or allergy that does not fit the patient in front of them.
beats: A nurse sees an allergy that the patient denies
A result belongs to a different age and sex
Registration reports two patients with one record number
A tip arrives through the patient safety hotline

phaseArc.title: Scope the overlay
phaseArc.goal: The team finds how many charts and what content are affected, and what to freeze.
beats: A merge tool log shows a recent bulk merge
Documentation was entered on both patients
Orders were released for the wrong patient
A decision to hold results until validated

phaseArc.title: Contain and correct
phaseArc.goal: Corrections must be sequenced; an unmerge is risky and the legal record must stay intact.
beats: HIM asks how to preserve the legal record
A physician demands immediate unmerge
Downstream systems have already received the wrong identity
A patient is told something that was wrong

phaseArc.title: Verify and notify
phaseArc.goal: The team verifies downstream systems, files safety reports and decides who must be notified, including the privacy office.
beats: A disclosure to the wrong patient triggers a breach assessment
A report to the patient safety organization is drafted
The post-event safety review is scheduled

decisionPointExamples: unmerge now with a chance of further errors, or freeze the charts and work on paper
notify the affected patients immediately, or finish the assessment first
hold all results for the two patients until validated, or release with a warning banner
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a merge log, an audit trail entry, two registration times, a demographic mismatch, a duplicate-record report
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: downstream systems that kept the wrong identity, a merge that cannot be reversed in one step, a legal record that must not be altered
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the health information management director and the patient safety officer
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: The four-factor breach risk assessment applies when PHI reached the wrong person. All names, record numbers and dates are fictional.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Clinical decision support firing wrongly
addedThreatFamilies.description: After a build change or update, alerts fire for the wrong patients, fire constantly, or stop firing. Clinicians either override everything or lose a safety net.

phaseArc.title: First complaints
phaseArc.goal: Ambiguity: scattered clinician complaints about alerts, none of them conclusive.
beats: A pharmacist reports alerts for the wrong allergy class
An override rate chart is unusually high
A clinician asks to turn alerts off
An analyst finds a build change from last night

phaseArc.title: Is it unsafe
phaseArc.goal: Informatics and clinical leaders decide whether to disable, roll back or keep the alerts.
beats: A near miss is reported
The CMIO is asked for a clinical sign-off
A rollback needs a change window
Unit leaders hear conflicting messages

phaseArc.title: Roll back and communicate
phaseArc.goal: The rollback and the message to clinicians are sequenced, with monitoring in between.
beats: A rollback restores some but not all rules
A message goes to clinicians with unclear scope
Pharmacy asks for a manual double check

phaseArc.title: Review
phaseArc.goal: The team reviews exposure, files safety events and sets change-control improvements.
beats: A list of affected patients is produced
The change control gap is named
A committee review is scheduled

decisionPointExamples: disable the alert class now and lose a safety net, or keep it on and accept alert fatigue
roll back overnight with limited staff, or wait for the change window
notify all clinicians now with partial scope, or wait for the full scope
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a change ticket, an override report, an alert log, a rule version number, a build migration note
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a rollback that restores only some rules, a change window nobody can staff, conflicting messages from two leaders
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the CMIO, pharmacy informatics and the EHR vendor
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Clinical content is plausible but not a clinical reference; keep it marked as exercise content.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Device network loss or vulnerability
addedThreatFamilies.description: Networked medical devices (infusion pumps, monitors, central stations, imaging) lose their network, or a vulnerability forces isolation. Manual alternatives and device inventories decide the outcome.

phaseArc.title: Signals
phaseArc.goal: Ambiguity: alarms or telemetry gaps on one unit, and a vendor or regulator notice.
beats: Central station shows a unit offline
A pump drug library update fails on a unit
A manufacturer advisory arrives by email
Biomed cannot match the advisory to the inventory

phaseArc.title: Isolate or not
phaseArc.goal: Isolation protects the network and removes a capability; clinical leaders weigh manual alternatives.
beats: Biomed proposes isolating a device class
Nurses are asked to monitor manually
A unit lacks spare equipment
A vendor offers a patch window

phaseArc.title: Sustain
phaseArc.goal: Manual monitoring, staffing and patching go on together.
beats: A near miss at a pump
Vendor support asks for remote access
Staffing is stretched

phaseArc.title: Restore and verify
phaseArc.goal: Devices return in order and are verified.
beats: A device fails verification
The safety review begins

decisionPointExamples: isolate the device class and run manual monitoring, or keep it connected and accept the vulnerability window
accept the vendor remote access for the patch, or refuse and wait for onsite support
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a device inventory mismatch, a vendor advisory, a network scan result, a central station log
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: devices missing from the inventory, a patch that needs a reboot, a vendor that wants remote access
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the clinical engineering director and the device manufacturer
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Device names are generic; no manufacturer branding. Safety communications are from the exercise, not a regulator.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Clinical third-party or hosted service failure
addedThreatFamilies.description: A cloud EHR host, claims clearinghouse, telehealth platform, hosted lab or a security-agent update fails or is breached, and the hospital cannot fix it itself.

phaseArc.title: Vendor silence
phaseArc.goal: Ambiguity: the hospital sees the failure before the vendor acknowledges it.
beats: Video visits fail to connect
The vendor status page is silent
Claims are rejected by the clearinghouse
Patients call the portal helpline

phaseArc.title: Dependence
phaseArc.goal: The team finds what depends on the vendor and what has no workaround.
beats: A list of dependent workflows is drafted
The contract has no recovery time commitment
A business associate notice is considered

phaseArc.title: Workaround and message
phaseArc.goal: Manual workarounds begin and messages go to patients and partners.
beats: A phone-based visit workaround is set up
A patient message is drafted
Counsel asks about notification duties

phaseArc.title: Return and review
phaseArc.goal: Service returns; backlogs are processed and the vendor review begins.
beats: A backlog of claims or visits
The vendor review is scheduled

decisionPointExamples: move patients to phone visits or cancel them
notify patients now, or wait for the vendor facts
invoke the contract escalation or stay quiet to avoid public attention
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a vendor status note, an error code, a claims rejection report, a service level report
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a vendor with no recovery commitment, a backlog that exceeds capacity, a contract clause that blocks escalation
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the vendor, the compliance office and counsel
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Name no real vendor. Third-party breach duties follow the business associate chain; counsel decides.

noiseExamples: a printer out of label stock on a unit unrelated to the failure
a password reset request from a visiting physician
a badge printer out of cards
a request to update a clinician photo in the directory
pressureExamples: a surgeon demanding the OR schedule be restored
a charge nurse asking if she can stop double charting on paper
a lab director asking which results can be trusted
counsel asking when the 60-day notification clock started
a reporter asking whether patient records were exposed
the state survey agency asking for a status report
